records.sourceFile: Exploring the effect of long naps on handball performance and heart rate variability.pdf

paper.citation: Nishida M, Yamamoto K, Murata Y, Ichinose A, Shioda K. Exploring the Effect of Long Naps on Handball Performance and Heart Rate Variability. Sports Med Int Open. 2021;5:E73-E80.
paper.abstract: Eleven male collegiate handball players completed a handball-specific test (turnaround runs, a loaded 10-m run and ball shooting) after no nap, a 20-min nap and a 60-min nap. Nap condition had no significant effect on performance, but after the long nap higher heart rate variability (RMSSD) during the nap correlated with faster loaded run time. After the long nap, poorer habitual sleep quality (higher Pittsburgh Sleep Quality Index score) also correlated with higher shooting accuracy.
paper.tldr: A 60-minute nap did not change handball-specific performance on average in this small group of collegiate players. Any link between nap length, sleep quality and shooting accuracy is exploratory and should not guide individual nap plans yet.
paper.methods: Eleven male collegiate handball players were randomly assigned, in a crossover design with at least one week between sessions, to a no-nap, 20-min nap or 60-min nap condition before a test of three 20-m turnaround runs, a 10-m run carrying a load and three shots at a 45 cm target. Naps and heart rate were recorded with Actiheart 5 monitors, HRV was analyzed in 5-min epochs, and the analysis used linear mixed-effects models and Spearman correlations.
paper.findings: Linear mixed models showed no significant condition effect or condition-by-trial interaction for the 20-m turnaround run, the 10-m load run or shooting accuracy. In the long-nap condition only, PSQI score (higher means poorer sleep) correlated positively with average shooting accuracy (rho = 0.658, p = 0.039) and RMSSD correlated negatively with average 10-m load run time (rho = -0.929, p < 0.001); neither correlation was significant after the short nap. HRV indices did not differ between short and long naps, and post-nap sleepiness (KSS) did not differ across the three conditions.
paper.limitations: The study had 11 men, one participant's nap data were excluded, and the authors state the results cannot be extrapolated to women. The abstract gives the PSQI correlation as rho = 0.636 with 'r = 0.048', while the Results and Table 3 give rho = 0.658 and p = 0.039; the abstract also claims a significant benefit of long naps for poor sleepers, and the Discussion says longer naps were 'likely more beneficial for 10-m turnaround runs', but Table 2 shows no significant condition effects and a slightly slower average turnaround time after the long nap (12.52 s) than the short nap (12.35 s). The tasks were simplified, habituation and day-to-day variability were noted, and several correlations were tested in a very small sample.
paper.practicalImplications: A single 60-minute nap did not change handball-specific performance compared with no nap or a 20-minute nap, so a nap should not be expected to produce a measurable performance gain by itself. The PSQI-accuracy correlation after long naps is a single exploratory finding in about 10 athletes, so it is a hypothesis for a larger controlled trial, not a basis for prescribing long naps to poor sleepers.
paper.athleteDev: A 60-minute nap did not improve handball-specific sprint, loaded run or shooting performance on average in these 11 collegiate players. The signals that poorer sleepers shot more accurately after a long nap, and that higher nap RMSSD went with faster loaded runs, are exploratory correlations that need a larger controlled trial before a nap plan is based on them.
paper.rtp: This study cannot inform return-to-sport decisions. It tests no injured or rehabilitating athletes and does not measure return-to-sport readiness, so it should not be used for that purpose.

records.sourceFile: Extended match time exacerbates fatigue and impacts physiological responses in male soccer players.pdf

paper.citation: Mohr M, Ermidis G, Jamustas AZ, Vigh-Larsen J, Poulios A, Draganidis D, et al. Extended Match Time Exacerbates Fatigue and Impacts Physiological Responses in Male Soccer Players. Med Sci Sports Exerc. 2022.
paper.abstract: In 20 competitive male players, the 30-minute extra-time period of 120-minute games was associated with lower running output, maximal speed and accelerations per minute than the first 90 minutes, with further declines in repeated-sprint and jump performance and muscle glycogen. The authors also report lower blood glucose and higher plasma ammonia and glycerol after extra time, and they conclude that metabolic disturbances are a major part of the fatigue response.
paper.tldr: Running output per minute, maximal speed and post-match sprint and jump performance were lower after 30 minutes of extra time than after 90 minutes, and muscle glycogen fell to very low levels in most fibers. Staff should plan for lower late-game output in 120-minute matches, but this analysis does not test fueling strategies.
paper.methods: Analysis of the first 120-minute game in each of two trials of a pre-registered crossover project (40 player observations, 30 with complete data), before any diet intervention, comparing the 90-minute and 120-minute time points within the match. Match tracking used 10 Hz GPS and heart rate, with countermovement jump, repeated-sprint tests, knee strength, blood sampling and vastus lateralis biopsies at baseline, 90 and 120 minutes, analyzed by repeated-measures ANOVA.
paper.findings: In Table 2, total distance per minute was 9.7% lower, maximal speed 10.1% lower and accelerations and decelerations per minute 18.3% and 16.8% lower in extra time than in the first 90 minutes, and successful passes and duels won also fell; high-intensity running per minute was 11.6% lower but is not flagged as significant in the table, and sprint distance per minute was essentially unchanged (-0.8%). Countermovement jump fell 19% at 90 minutes and 27% at 120 minutes against baseline, and muscle glycogen fell from 266 +/- 64 to 186 +/- 56 mmol/kg dry weight, with 82% of slow-twitch and 78% of fast-twitch fibers completely or almost empty after 120 minutes. Blood glucose fell 13% after extra time against baseline and 90 minutes, and plasma ammonia (+191% vs baseline) and glycerol (+137%) rose further, which the authors link to fatigue.
paper.limitations: Extra time is compared with the same match's first 90 minutes, so the effect is confounded with cumulative time on the pitch, and players knew extra time was coming, which the authors acknowledge. The repeated-sprint test and biopsies before extra time may have lowered glycogen (the authors' own caveat), up to 30 observations pooled from 20 players are analyzed as if independent, and sample sizes vary by outcome (n = 30, 25, 19 and 11). Reported values conflict in places: the Results text gives high-intensity running and sprinting as p < 0.01 while Table 2 does not flag them and their effect sizes are trivial to small; maximal speed is 11% in the abstract versus 10.1% in Table 2; depleted fibers are about 75% (abstract), 76% (Discussion) or 82% and 78% (Results); and the Results report glycogen correlated with the sprint fatigue index (r = -0.56) while the Discussion says no such association was shown.
paper.practicalImplications: Staff could expect lower running output, slower maximal speed and weaker post-match sprint and jump performance in the final 30 minutes of a 120-minute game, and plan recovery and substitutions with that in mind. Because glycogen and blood glucose were low at 120 minutes, recovery planning for players who play extra time could account for fuel status, but this analysis did not test any fueling intervention.
paper.athleteDev: Total distance per minute fell about 10% and maximal speed about 10% in the extra-time period, with fewer accelerations and decelerations and weaker post-match sprint and jump tests. Performance staff planning for 120-minute matches or cup schedules could expect lower late-game output and plan rotation and recovery around it.
paper.rtp: This study cannot inform return-to-sport decisions. It enrolled players free of recent injury and tests match fatigue in healthy players, so it does not assess rehabilitation or readiness after injury.

paper.citation: Robson-Ansley PJ, Gleeson M, Ansley L. Fatigue management in the preparation of Olympic athletes. J Sports Sci. 2009;27(13):1409-1420.
paper.abstract: Narrative review of practical methods for monitoring and managing fatigue in Olympic athletes. The authors assess the scientific merit of self-assessed training load, self-scored questionnaires, saliva and blood diagnostic markers, nutrition and hydration strategies, and short-term recovery methods. They conclude that sufficient nutrition, hydration and rest are the best-supported strategies for optimising recovery in Olympic athletes.
paper.tldr: For Olympic athletes, the best-supported fatigue management is adequate rest, sleep, carbohydrate intake and hydration. Session RPE and brief questionnaires are practical monitoring tools, but no single blood or saliva marker reliably identifies overreaching.
paper.methods: Narrative review of training-load methods, questionnaires, performance tests, blood and saliva markers, nutrition, hydration and recovery modalities, drawing on studies in trained and elite athletes. The Methods section does not describe a search strategy or study selection.
paper.findings: The authors describe session RPE multiplied by duration as a simple training-load method that gives similar results to TRIMP except at high intensity, citing a recommendation to keep weekly load below 4000 to 5000 arbitrary units. They report that POMS and DALDA questionnaires are practical indicators of training stress, and that no single reliable diagnostic marker of overreaching or underperformance syndrome exists, although the plasma cortisol to testosterone ratio is considered a good indicator of the overreached state. They give carbohydrate targets from 5 to 7 g/kg/day for light to moderate training up to 10 to 12 g/kg/day for extreme training, and report that active recovery speeds lactate removal but its benefit for subsequent performance is questionable, with little evidence supporting massage.
paper.limitations: The review has no described search method, so it cannot be checked for completeness. The authors note that there is little literature on recovery strategies in elite athletes, and that the outcomes used in recovery studies (lactate clearance or muscle soreness) may not apply to them. Evidence on long-term daily questionnaire use is scarce.
paper.practicalImplications: Track session RPE and a brief mood or stress questionnaire over several days rather than relying on one score. Schedule at least one passive rest day per week, protect sleep, and use earplugs or quieter rooms where noise disturbs sleep. Match carbohydrate intake to training load, and use urinary ketones and urine colour as practical checks on carbohydrate intake and hydration. The authors find no evidence of benefit for massage, stretching, cryotherapy alone, hydrotherapy or active recovery, and some evidence that compression garments may help.
paper.athleteDev: Session RPE and questionnaires can show whether training load is being absorbed, and the review's guidance on rest, sleep and carbohydrate intake can be used to adjust the load. The paper gives no sport-specific training prescription and no outcome data from a training intervention.
paper.rtp: The review concerns fatigue after training and competition, not recovery from injury, and it gives no return-to-sport criteria. Its general guidance on rest, sleep and nutrition cannot be used to clear an athlete to return to play.

records.sourceFile: Fundamentals or icing on Top of the Cake - A narrative review of recovery strategies and devices for athletes.pdf

paper.citation: Driller M, Leabeater A. Fundamentals or Icing on Top of the Cake? A Narrative Review of Recovery Strategies and Devices for Athletes. Sports. 2023;11:213.
paper.abstract: This narrative review ranks recovery strategies by the strength of their evidence, from meta-analyses to case reports. The authors report a high level of positive evidence for foam rolling, compression garments, cryotherapy, photobiomodulation, hydrotherapy and active recovery. Sauna, recovery boots or sleeves, occlusion cuffs and massage guns have lower-level and mixed evidence, and the review offers guidance for using strategies across season phases.
paper.tldr: Foam rolling, compression garments, cold water immersion, cryotherapy, photobiomodulation and active recovery have the strongest evidence in this review. Sleep, nutrition and periodisation should be optimised before adding recovery devices.
paper.methods: Narrative review. No search strategy is described. Recovery strategies were grouped by the level of evidence available, from meta-analyses and systematic reviews down to small trials and case reports.
paper.findings: Foam rolling and compression garments are reported to reduce soreness and improve range of motion, but few studies link these to athletic performance. Cold water immersion supports acute recovery, while the cited meta-analysis of eight studies found that regular use after resistance training may attenuate maximal strength adaptations. Sauna, recovery boots or sleeves, float tanks, occlusion cuffs and massage guns have limited or mixed evidence, and two case reports describe serious illness or injury after massage gun use.
paper.limitations: The review does not describe how sources were selected, so its evidence grading cannot be reproduced. The authors acknowledge that many strategies have been tested only in small trials or case reports, that performance evidence is sparse, and that the chronic effects of most modalities are largely unknown.
paper.practicalImplications: Check sleep, nutrition and training periodisation before adding recovery devices, since the authors position these as the foundation. Foam rolling, compression garments and cold water immersion can be used for soreness and perceived recovery, with timing adjusted to the season. Sauna, massage guns, occlusion cuffs and recovery boots have weaker evidence and should be used with caution.
paper.athleteDev: Use strategies with stronger evidence for soreness and perceived recovery, and do not expect them to raise performance on their own. The review suggests cold water immersion may suit in-season or competition periods, while repeated use after resistance training may blunt strength adaptation.
paper.rtp: This review does not study return to sport or injury rehabilitation, so it cannot guide return-to-play decisions. Its mention of sauna for injury rehabilitation is a cited claim, not evidence from the review.

records.sourceFile: Greater Effect of East versus West              Travel on Jet Lag, Sleep, and Team Sport Performance.pdf

paper.citation: Fowler PM, Knez W, Crowcroft S, Mendham AE, Miller J, Sargent C, et al. Greater Effect of East versus West Travel on Jet Lag, Sleep, and Team Sport Performance. Medicine & Science in Sports & Exercise. 2017;49(12):2548-2561.
paper.abstract: Ten physically trained men were tested for four days before, and four days after, a 21-hour westward trip from Australia to Qatar and a return eastward trip across eight time zones. Measures included countermovement jump, 20-m sprint, Yo-Yo IR1, sleep monitoring, and jet lag, fatigue and motivation ratings. The authors report that east travel had a greater detrimental effect on sleep, jet lag, fatigue, motivation and maximal and intermittent sprint performance, particularly within 72 hours of arrival.
paper.tldr: In 10 trained men, travelling east across eight time zones reduced sleep and sprint performance more than travelling west did, and jet lag and fatigue lasted longer. The authors suggest arriving about 96 hours before competition, a recommendation from a small, non-counterbalanced study.
paper.methods: Ten physically trained men (age 20.6 ± 2.7 years) were tested at 0900 and 1700 h on four days before outbound travel (BASE), for four days after a westward trip from Australia to Qatar (WEST), and for four days after the eastward return (EAST), with a pre-return day used as an internal control. Countermovement jump, 20-m sprint and Yo-Yo IR1 performance, jet lag, fatigue, motivation and physical feeling ratings, and wrist-monitor and diary sleep data were analysed with linear mixed models.
paper.findings: Across the four days, sleep duration and time in bed were reduced after east travel compared with BASE and WEST (P < 0.05), with later sleep onset and offset, and mean jet lag, function (fatigue and mental performance) and motivation ratings were worse after east than west travel. Yo-Yo IR1 distance fell after east travel on day 1 but rose after west travel (P < 0.001), and 20-m sprint times were slower on day 2 after east than west travel (P = 0.03). Countermovement jump and sprint performance were reduced after both directions, with CMJ deficits greatest on day 3, and after west travel mean jet lag, function and motivation ratings were also worse than at BASE.
paper.limitations: The direction order was not counterbalanced, which the authors acknowledge, so the east-west difference cannot be separated from order effects, and arrival time of day also differed (morning after west, 2220 h after east). The group is 10 men, interindividual variation was large, and only large effect sizes are reported. The Discussion calls the effects of west travel negligible and says west travel had no effect on sleep, but the Results report worse jet lag, function and motivation after west travel than at BASE, and the 96-hour arrival recommendation is extrapolated from CMJ recovery rather than tested.
paper.practicalImplications: Expect the largest sleep, motivation and sprint decrements after east travel, mainly in the first 48 to 72 hours, but do not treat west travel as harmless, since CMJ and sprint performance and perceived jet lag were also worse than baseline after it. The authors' suggestion of arriving at least 96 hours before competition was not tested in this study and should be treated as a hypothesis to check locally.
paper.athleteDev: Expect sprint and sleep decrements after eastward travel, mainly in the first 48 to 72 hours after arrival, and lower-body power deficits for up to about 3 to 4 days after travel in either direction. The 96-hour arrival suggestion is the authors' untested recommendation from 10 trained men, not a validated threshold for elite players.
paper.rtp: The participants were healthy trained men and no injury, rehabilitation or return-to-sport outcomes were measured. The study cannot guide clearance or return-to-play decisions.

records.sourceFile: Hamstrings passive and active shear modulus - Implications of conventional static stretching and warmup.pdf

paper.citation: Pimenta R, Correia JP, Vaz JR, Veloso AP, Herzog W. Hamstrings passive and active shear modulus: implications of conventional static stretching and warmup. J Sci Med Sport. 2024.
paper.abstract: Forty physically active men without hamstring injury history were tested before and after a 5-minute static stretching protocol or a running-style warm-up, using shear wave elastography at rest and at 20% of maximal isometric contraction. After stretching, knee flexion strength fell by 18.3%, passive shear modulus did not change, and active shear modulus rose in biceps femoris short head and fell in semimembranosus. After the warm-up, passive shear modulus did not change, and active shear modulus fell only in semitendinosus, a change within measurement error.
paper.tldr: Five minutes of static stretching changed the active stiffness of two hamstring muscles in opposite directions and reduced knee flexion strength by 18%. A running-style warm-up left passive stiffness unchanged and changed active stiffness only trivially.
paper.methods: Two separate experiments in 40 physically active men (20 per experiment), each completing one laboratory session with pre and post measures and no control condition. Shear modulus of the biceps femoris long and short heads, semimembranosus and semitendinosus was measured by shear wave elastography at rest and at 20% of maximal isometric knee flexion, before and after passive static stretching (five 60-second repetitions) in one experiment or a warm-up of treadmill running, calisthenics and skipping in the other. The authors describe the design as an observational cross-sectional study.
paper.findings: After stretching, knee flexion maximal torque fell from 98.9 to 80.8 Nm (18.3%, p<0.001), and passive shear modulus showed no change (p=0.996). At 20% contraction, active shear modulus fell in semimembranosus and rose in biceps femoris short head, and the pre-post difference between them rose from 3.8 to 39.3 kPa (p<0.001, d=1.66). After warm-up, maximal torque rose 1.4% (p=0.03, d=0.06), passive shear modulus was unchanged, and semitendinosus active shear modulus fell from 65.3 to 60.3 kPa (p=0.035, d=0.4), within a standard error of measurement of 10.54 kPa.
paper.limitations: Stretching and warm-up were tested in different groups with no control condition, so the two protocols cannot be compared directly. The authors state that the active measurement was made at one contraction level, that muscle temperature was not measured after warm-up, and that other synergists crossing the knee were not measured; passive measures were taken with the hamstrings slack (hip neutral, knee 30 degrees).
paper.practicalImplications: Five minutes of static stretching changed active shear modulus in opposite directions for the biceps femoris short head and semimembranosus, and reduced knee flexion strength by 18%. Do not expect the running-style warm-up to change hamstring passive or active stiffness in this sample. The functional meaning of these shifts is not known, so do not use them as a training or injury-prevention target.
paper.athleteDev: The study shows that a running-style warm-up did not meaningfully change hamstring shear modulus in physically active men, and that stretching reduced knee flexion torque for the period tested. No performance outcome was measured.
paper.rtp: The study cannot inform return to sport. It included no injured participants and measured no return-to-play or rehabilitation outcomes, so it cannot show when hamstring stiffness returns to normal after injury.

records.sourceFile: Higher Levels of Morning and Daytime Light Exposure Associated with Positive Sleep Indices in Professional Team Sport Athletes.pdf

paper.citation: Stevenson S, Suppiah H, Ruddy J, Murphy S, Driller M. Higher Levels of Morning and Daytime Light Exposure Associated with Positive Sleep Indices in Professional Team Sport Athletes. Nature and Science of Sleep. 2024;16:1279-1290.
paper.abstract: Seventeen professional male Australian football players wore a wrist actigraph and a wearable light sensor for 14 days, and completed sleep questionnaires at the end. Morning light was linked to longer total sleep time, daytime light to higher subjective sleep quality, and evening light to higher Athlete Sleep Screening Questionnaire scores. The authors conclude that athletes should be educated on optimizing light exposure.
paper.tldr: Elite Australian football players with more light in the morning and during the day recorded longer sleep or better sleep quality, while brighter evening light went with more sleep-problem scores. These are correlations in 17 players over two weeks, so they support sleep education rather than showing that light changes sleep.
paper.methods: Observational study of 17 male professional players at one club during pre-season. Wrist actigraphy and collar-worn melanopic light sensors recorded sleep and light for 14 days, with questionnaires (ASBQ, ASSQ, B-PSQI) completed at the end; light was summed into morning, daytime and evening windows. Repeated-measures correlation was used for nightly sleep measures and Pearson correlation for questionnaire and well-being measures.
paper.findings: Morning light was correlated with total sleep time (repeated-measures r = 0.26, p = 0.001). Daytime light was correlated with subjective sleep quality (r = 0.48, reported as p = 0.05), and evening light with ASSQ global score (r = 0.52, p = 0.04). Other light and sleep or well-being correlations were not significant, and the sample had a mean sleep latency of about 7 minutes and mean sleep regularity index of 79.
paper.limitations: The sample was small and came from one club, and the design is correlational, so causation cannot be inferred. Light was measured by a collar-worn sensor that may not reflect light at the eye, its validity rests on unpublished laboratory observations, and sleep came from a consumer wrist device. The abstract reports morning light with total sleep time as r = 0.31, while Table 3 and the results give r = 0.26; this review uses the table value. The daytime sleep-quality result sits at p = 0.05 against a stated p < 0.05 threshold, and the athletes trained mostly outdoors, which may not apply to indoor-based athletes.
paper.practicalImplications: Use these results to support education on getting light in the morning and during the day and reducing light before bed, as the authors recommend. The findings are correlations and do not show that changing a player's light exposure will improve their sleep, so do not present them as a validated sleep intervention.
paper.athleteDev: In 17 elite Australian football players during pre-season, more morning and daytime light went with longer sleep and better self-rated sleep, while brighter evening light went with more sleep-problem scores. Use these links to frame light habits as part of sleep education rather than as a proven sleep intervention.
paper.rtp: This study cannot inform return to sport. It measured sleep and light exposure in pre-season players and includes no injury, rehabilitation or return-to-play outcomes.
